item.title: UK announces sanctions on West Bank settlements prompting furious Israeli response
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c4g7zen0vveo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
UK announces sanctions on West Bank settlements prompting furious Israeli response - Published The UK has announced sanctions on illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, accusing Israel's government of turning a blind eye to the "ethnic cleansing" of Palestinians by settlers. Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said the move marked the "beginning of a new approach" to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, which "not only calls out injustice and suffering but acts". Israel's Foreign Minister Gideon Saar responded by accusing him of spreading an "outrageous lie" and announced counter-measures including shutting the UK's consulate in East Jerusalem. The UK sanctions will ban settlement goods but also act against companies and individuals providing services for settlement expansion. - In West Bank, date farmers weigh impact of UK sanctions on Israeli settlers - Published11 hours ago - How Israel is expanding settlements in drive to reshape West Bank - Published21 August The sanctions were launched alongside France and Canada, which in a joint statement with the UK said the action "marks a further turning point in our approach to protecting the two-state solution". Settlements are illegal under international law, and there has been a rise in violence towards Palestinians in the West Bank by settlers in recent months. In a statement to MPs, Miliband said: "The British government agrees that there is ethnic cleansing of Palestinians in areas of the West Bank, perpetrated by settler terrorists. "And all too often the Israeli government has turned a blind eye to this and worse, members of it have made statements and taken actions to support the forced displacement of Palestinians." He said ethnic cleansing was defined by the UN as a "purposeful policy designed by one ethnic or religious group to remove by violent means another ethnic or religious group from certain areas". Miliband said the official view of the government was that the Israeli occupation of the West Bank was unlawful because of the "entrenchment of its control, its intention to extend permanent sovereignty, and its expansionist agenda via illegal settlements". He said this position, which is in line with a 2024 advisory opinion from the International Court of Justice, should be reflected in the UK's "economic relationship" with the occupied West Bank. As a result, over the next six to nine months, the UK will introduce "a new comprehensive sanctions regime", he said. The foreign secretary also announced a ban on advertising illegal West Bank settlements in the UK. "The sanctions regime will target illegal settlements and settlement expansion, not Israel," Miliband added. Later on Tuesday, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the targeted measures were "aimed not at the Israeli people, but in support of the two-state solution". Announcing the closure of the consulate - which represents the UK government in Jerusalem, the West Bank and Gaza - Israel's Foreign Minister Saar said at a press conference: "We know that we have many friends in Britain. "Unfortunately, we have a hostile Labour government that is consistently operating against the State of Israel, and it has left us no choice but to respond to its hostile actions." He added that 11 UK MPs, including Jeremy Corbyn, Diane Abbott and all five sitting Green Party MPs, would be banned from entering Israel, accusing them of "antisemitic and anti-Israel activity". The UK also issued a joint statement with 11 other countries; France, Canada, Denmark, Spain, Finland, Ireland, Iceland, Norway, Poland, Portugal and Sweden. It said the group was unequivocally committed to the two-state solution and would introduce national measures or support European restrictions on trading goods with West Bank settlements. The UK announcement comes after Israel opened up tenders for the construction of some 1,200 settlement homes in the so-called E1 area - a strategically important area east of Jerusalem. The plans have drawn widespread international condemnation. Israel has held off on plans to build in the area for decades under global pressure. Miliband told the Commons the UK's "new approach" was necessary because plans for the E1 development in the West Bank would render a two-state solution "unviable" by "cutting through the heart of Palestine". Elsewhere, he said the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, which triggered the Gaza war, carried "terrible echoes of the centuries of persecution of the Jewish people" and stressed Israel had "the right to protect its people and defend its territory". However, he added, "that cannot justify what has happened in Gaza". He said: "International humanitarian law imposes clear rules for states fighting wars, including to ensure access to food and medical supplies, to avoid mass displacement of civilians, and to avoid the targeting of civilians. Serious and international violations of this law, if proven, amount to war crimes. "What has occurred, including the actions of the IDF (Israel Defense Forces), have been examined in depth by a number of organisations, including the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry. "The conclusions of these reports represent increasing evidence that war crimes appear to have been committed, and we support legal processes to determine this." He added it was up to international courts to determine if Israel had committed genocide in Gaza. Israel's leaders have consistently rejected allegations of genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes. They have insisted that Israeli forces have operated in accordance with international law. Miliband began his statement to the Commons by referring to his Jewish roots and childhood experiences of visiting Israel, as well as recent antisemitic attacks in the UK. He described himself as "a proud British Jew" and outlined his steadfast support for the state of Israel. He said: "My personal story and that of thousands of British Jews is one of the many reasons why I say to anyone here or around the world who questions Israel's right to exist as a homeland for the Jewish people - you are wrong, and we will call you out whenever you engage in this attempt at the erasure of Israel." But the UK's Chief Rabbi Sir Ephraim Mirvis said it was a "truly a dark day for British Jews", saying the sanctions were "little more than political flag bearing for mendacious anti-Israel rhetoric" that would embolden people who "use hatred as a weapon against Jews". The Board of Deputies of British Jews expressed "deep regret" over Tuesday's announcement, and urged both the UK and Israeli governments to "avoid pursuing what appear to be party interests over national interests". In an interview with Jewish News, external after speaking in the Commons, Miliband said "any person who targets British Jews because of the actions of the Israeli government is an antisemite in my view", a position which he said was "shared across the House of Commons". He said the response from the Israeli government had been "deeply regrettable". Responding in the Commons, Conservative shadow foreign secretary Tom Tugendhat claimed ministers were "enacting policies that the Foreign Office knows won't work". He agreed that illegal settlements were wrong and "some Israeli ministers have indulged in hateful propaganda and incitement" but added "this isn't about Israel alone and it certainly isn't about reducing the complexity of the region to a single sentence. Sadly, the government is in the process of doing just that". Israel's foreign minister Saar said on Tuesday evening he had spoken with Tugendhat and Tory leader Kemi Badenoch, thanking them "for their firm opposition to the hostile Labour government's announcement today and its series of anti-Israel policies since taking office". He also said British representatives from the International Gaza Support Center in Kiryat Gat in southern Israel would be removed, and UK activities to train Palestinian Authority forces in Judea and Samaria - how the Israeli government refers to the West Bank - would be terminated. Speaking earlier on Tuesday, the country's President Isaac Herzog said the decision would "fall on the wrong side of history", adding: "In the current context, it would be a gross interference in the democratic elections of a sovereign nation." Herzog said the move would directly harm Palestinians and urged foreign governments to turn towards "constructive dialogue" and cooperation, adding "sanctions are not a solution". US Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters the White House had no comment on the joint action, adding that "obviously we're not going to do what the UK did". Earlier, Donald Trump's ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee earlier told the BBC that the US - Israel's most powerful ally - would "without a doubt" respond to the expected sanctions, warning of a "huge economic impact on British businesses". He suggested action could be taken by individual US states as well as at a central, federal level. The Palestinian presidency welcomed the UK's decision, saying it was "an important step towards confronting Israel's colonial system and its violations against the Palestinian people". As part of the UK announcement, Miliband also announced sanctions on the financing wing of Lebanon's Hezbollah, the Iran-backed armed group. New sanctions in line with the US and European Union were also announced on Iran. The intervention comes almost a year after Sir Keir Starmer's government recognised a state of Palestine, and said the UK had a moral responsibility to support a peaceful future for Israelis and Palestinians. Israel rejects a two-state solution. It says any final settlement must be the result of negotiations with the Palestinians, and statehood should not be a precondition. The Palestinian Authority backs a two-state solution but Palestinian armed group Hamas does not because it is opposed to the existence of Israel. Hamas says that it could accept an interim Palestinian state based on 1967 de facto borders, without officially recognising Israel, if refugees were given the right to return. Israel has built about 160 settlements housing 700,000 Jews since it occupied the West Bank and East Jerusalem during the 1967 Middle East war. An estimated 3.3 million Palestinians live alongside them. There has been a surge in attacks by settlers on Palestinians and their property in the West Bank since the start of the Gaza war, which was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on Israel on 7 October 2023.

item.title: Paul Adams: British-Israeli relations at lowest ebb in decades
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c5ydlex9yn3o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Paul Adams: British-Israeli relations at lowest ebb in decades - Published Israel's furious response to the British government's decision to ban trade with Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank testifies to just how important this moment is. Britain took the brunt of Israel's anger, but the fact that 12 countries chose to move together clearly sharpened the sense of outrage. Officials in London always knew that such a dramatic shift in policy towards Israel-Palestine was going to elicit a hostile response, but seemed taken aback by the speed and ferocity of Israel's reaction. The closure of the UK's consulate in East Jerusalem, which serves the West Bank and deals directly with the Palestinian Authority in Ramallah, and the removal of British representatives from the International Gaza Support Centre, the body set up last year to co-ordinate stabilisation and relief efforts in the Gaza Strip, are very hostile moves. They tell you that Israel is deeply troubled by Tuesday's action by the UK and 11 other countries, which include France, Spain and Canada. Products manufactured in settlements may not represent a significant proportion of Israel's exports, but the political symbolism of singling these out for special treatment is powerful. For decades, the British and other governments have regarded settlements in occupied Palestinian territory as illegal but stopped short of banning products grown or manufactured there. Now, having announced that Britain agrees with the 2024 International Court of Justice ruling that the occupation as a whole - including Israel's military presence - is unlawful, Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband says the government's economic relationships must reflect that. Hence the ban, not just on products but also on companies that provide construction, infrastructure or finance to settlements. The measures, which also include restrictions on arms sales that "materially contribute to the occupation", go further than many expected. And it's not just the actions - it's the language of the foreign secretary's heartfelt, sometimes deeply personal statement that is so striking. As a "proud British Jew... unwavering in my support for the state of Israel," Miliband spoke more directly and starkly than practically any of his predecessors. That a British foreign secretary should say that "settler terrorism is rampant" and was responsible for the "ethnic cleansing" of Palestinians in parts of the West Bank, while the Israeli government "turned a blind eye to this" is truly remarkable. Miliband calls this a "reset" in British policy. At times today, it felt like a radical rethink, and it leaves British-Israeli relations at their lowest ebb for decades. Yes, the heated, febrile atmosphere that invariably accompanies an impending Israeli election may have contributed to Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar's brutal response, but most Israelis will have shared his sense of outrage. Many Israelis find the violent, messianic ideology of some settlers deeply problematic. Some see them as a national embarrassment. But that's not the same as saying they agree that settlements, built on land captured during the 1967 Six Day War, are illegal. Most would disagree violently with the former prime minister, Ehud Olmert, who last year accused his successor Benjamin Netanyahu of turning Israel into an international pariah. But they can feel the walls of international opprobrium closing in - from protests at Eurovision or sporting events, to international arrest warrants being issued against their leaders and now to bans on settlement products - and that makes them anxious and defensive. For the Palestinians, on the other hand, this feels like progress. The Palestinian foreign ministry commended the countries adopting sanctions but called for "urgent, concrete measures" to stop Israel's "illegal settlement enterprise". In London, the Palestinian ambassador Dr Husam Zomlot called the government's decision "a turning point in the UK-Palestine relationship". Britain's "courageous steps", he said, would help pave the way for the independence of the State of Palestine on the 1967 borders, with East Jerusalem as its capital. But Zomlot knows that the reality of Israel's 59-year occupation has not ended, or even substantially changed. The prospects for a viable Palestinian state remain vanishingly small, and there's little immediate sign that concerted action by 12 countries will reverse Israel's seemingly inexorable takeover of the West Bank. Only the United States has that kind of influence, should it choose to wield it. In 1991, President George HW Bush and his steely Secretary of State James Baker threatened to withhold $10bn (£7.4bn) in loan guarantees from the government of Prime Minister Yitzhak Shamir, when the famously tough Shamir refused to promise that it wouldn't be used to finance settlement activity in the occupied territories. But Donald Trump has so far shown no desire to curb Benjamin Netanyahu's settlement plans. Some parts of Trump's MAGA movement have turned against Israel in recent years, but the US ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, is a fervent Christian Zionist who shares Israel's view that the West Bank was promised to the Jews by God. So Tuesday's action by the UK and its partners pits them not just against Israel but also against Israel's backer-in-chief in Washington. - Published11 hours ago

item.title: US slaps import ban on Canadian alcohol and other goods
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c99dm1000p7o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
US slaps import ban on Canadian alcohol and other goods - Published The US is banning a slew of Canadian products, including alcoholic spirits, dairy goods and motor vehicles, as Canadian retaliatory tariffs on American goods come into force. In a series of executive orders on Tuesday, US President Donald Trump said that Canada is "discriminating" against the United States and outlined the import ban, to begin 29 September. Earlier on Tuesday, Canada Prime Minister Mark Carney said in a video address that his country's pivot away from the US as its largest trading partner "will come at a cost". Both US and Canadian officials have said they would like to strike a trade deal, but no new talks have been scheduled since negotiations collapsed in late August. The BBC has contacted the office of the Prime Minister of Canada, Mark Carney, for comment. The White House's new sanctions are the latest strike in a months-long trade war between the US and Canada. The sides have historically been close allies, with each a key business partner to the other. The US is Canada's largest trading partner - generally more than two-thirds of its total exports go to its neighbour. On the other hand, Canada is the US' second-largest trading partner, after Mexico, although its exports are far more diversified. Business owners on both sides of the border have expressed fears over the trade war's fallout. Many expect prices of goods to rise and the number of customers to fall. Last month, the White House had imposed 50% tariffs on around $20bn (£14.8bn) of Canadian goods after several rounds of talks had broken down. Those tariffs hit sectors including Canada's furniture and wine industries, as well as sporting and fishing equipment businesses. Canada responded with dollar-for-dollar retaliatory tariffs on US goods like steel, clothing and furniture. The counter-duties came into effect after midnight on Tuesday. Canada is "discriminating" against US businesses by restricting the distribution of US goods while not doing the same to such products from other countries, the White House said when announcing the new import restrictions on Tuesday. The response targets various alcoholic drinks and dairy products like whey, according to a series of White House statements signed by the president. On Monday, Trump hinted at more trade restrictions to come, warning Canadian aircraft company Bombardier that it would no longer be able to sell its products in the US unless it moves manufacturing there. Trump has long believed that tariffs will help reduce trade imbalances between the US and other countries, but his wide-ranging tariffs scheme has upset many of the States' traditional allies. Tension between the US and Canada have now also expanded beyond tariffs. In August, Trump ordered Lake Ontario to be renamed as Lake America, resulting in uproar from Canadians and some Americans. item.title: 'Constantly on my mind' - 9/11 agony goes on for bereaved, 25 years on
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/clyrjw1yj75o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
'Constantly on my mind' - 9/11 agony goes on for bereaved, 25 years on - Published The US government has described it as the "most egregious criminal act on American soil in modern history". But a quarter of a century on, the trial of its alleged mastermind is yet to begin and families of those killed fear that time for justice to be delivered is running out. Tom Resta's brother John and his wife Sylvia, who was seven months pregnant, were among the almost 3,000 people killed on 11 September 2001 when hijackers flew planes into the World Trade Center in New York City and the Pentagon in Virginia. Another crashed in a field in Pennsylvania after the passengers fought back. The couple had been preparing their unborn baby's nursery, painting it with characters from the children's television show Blue's Clues in the days before 9/11. They had dreamed of having a baby and doted on the children of friends and family. On the day of the attacks, the couple - both traders - were working on the 92nd floor of the north tower of the World Trade Center. "After all this time, it still chokes me up," Resta told the BBC through tears. While 25 years have passed, he said 9/11 was "almost constantly" on his mind. - New Yorkers were 'lied' to about toxic air after 9/11 attacks, says Mamdani - Published8 hours ago - New videos of man in 9/11 lawsuit reveal extremist links - Published1 day ago Resta has been to the US naval base of Guantanamo Bay four times to watch complex pre-trial proceedings for alleged 9/11 mastermind Khalid Sheikh Mohammed and his co-defendants - a process he describes as "laborious and tedious". A military prison was established on the base in south-eastern Cuba during the "war on terror" that followed the 9/11 attacks, and Mohammed - often referred to as KSM - has now been held there for 20 years without ever being convicted. Relatives of victims enter a lottery process to attend the proceedings in a high-security courtroom, where thick glass separates them and members of the press from the defendants. The pre-trial process has been going on for so long that it has now been presided over by five different military judges. Last month, as the 25th anniversary approached, there was a flurry of movement and something of a breakthrough, with a trial date set for Mohammed for June 2028. But Resta said he was bracing himself for further delays, and with so much time having passed, some of his relatives feared they would not live long enough to see the trial. "My father will be 98 in November, and I don't think he's expecting to see it. I have a lot of family members - aunts, uncles - that would all like to see it happen. But my parents in particular, I don't think they expect to live long enough," he said. "Hopefully all the defendants will still be alive by the time we get to trial. That's a big worry," he added. Resta's concerns that a trial could still be further delayed were shared by relatives of other 9/11 victims. Earlier this year, Stephan Gerhardt made his sixth trip to Guantanamo. He said seeing convictions for the death of his younger brother Ralph was vital for him, but something he wished he no longer had to think about. "I want to concentrate on the memories," he said. "I still have Ralph's car. I'm trying to restore it and get it in pristine shape again… We were recently visiting my parents, and we found some of his things that they were holding onto, and the emotion behind it is like, 'yeah, this is just some old stuff, but it belonged to my little brother'." Gerhardt said his "biggest concern" was that he wanted to see Mohammed and his alleged co-conspirators convicted before they died. "They're getting elderly… I don't want them to pass away without being convicted, because that would be an injustice to all the family members - that we captured these people, but we never got to try them and convict them for the mass murder that they did of our loved ones." Mohammed has been charged with offences including conspiracy and murder, with 2,976 victims listed on the charge sheet. He is accused of conceiving the idea of training pilots to fly commercial planes into buildings and taking those plans to Osama bin Laden, leader of the militant Islamist group al-Qaeda. He has previously said he planned the "9/11 operation from A to Z". But days after the trial date was set for 2028, the military judge threw out confessions made by Mohammed to FBI agents on Guantanamo Bay after he was brought there from secret CIA prisons known as "black sites", which he had been held in for years. In his ruling, the judge described Mohammed's treatment by the CIA as "extraordinary physical and mental abuse". He said the confessions were not voluntary and could not be used against Mohammed at trial. Experts say the torture of Mohammed and his alleged co-conspirators has been the main reason for the lengthy delays in the case. "Every single issue has been litigated through the issue of torture," said Kasey McCall-Smith, an international law professor at Edinburgh University. She said the defendants were subjected to "years of abuse", including waterboarding and stress positions. John Ryan, author of America's Trial: Torture and the 9/11 Case on Guantanamo Bay, said last month's ruling means prosecutors lose what they had described as their best evidence against Mohammed, but it is unclear how much it will impact the case. The prosecution has other evidence, Ryan says, including intercepted phone calls and secret recordings, but whether they can feature in the trial is not yet guaranteed. "Mohammad's team and the other defence teams will file motions to suppress some of these categories of evidence, as well." During the George W Bush administration, the US admitted using "enhanced interrogation techniques" to acquire information from suspects but said these methods saved lives and never amounted to torture. President Barack Obama banned them on his second day in office. Relatives of the victims say the torture of the defendants has so far blocked their right to justice. "If we would've not tortured them, the legal implications here would've been much, much simpler. They probably would've been sentenced to death a long time ago," said Gerhardt. "I can't control what the government did, and we've got to live with the impacts." Both Gerhardt and Resta travelled to Guantanamo in early 2025 when Mohammed and two of his co-defendants had been due to plead guilty under a controversial deal struck with US government prosecutors, through which they would not face a death penalty trial. The BBC was with them at the base when the pleas were paused at the last minute after the US government argued that to "deprive the government and the American people of a public trial as to the respondents' guilt and the possibility of capital punishment" would cause "irreparable" harm. Legal wrangling over the validity of the deal is continuing. - In court with the '9/11 mastermind', two decades after his arrest - Published10 January 2025 - The '9/11 mastermind' wants to plead guilty. Why is the US trying to stop him? - Published10 January 2025 Some victims' relatives viewed the deal as the only way through, while others criticised it as too lenient and lacking transparency. Resta said he had supported the deal to secure convictions. "My philosophy is these guys are not the kind of people that should be out walking the streets, but as far as I'm concerned, they can just stay right where they are. I just want them convicted," he said. Brett Eagleson, whose dad Bruce was killed in the attacks, said he wanted a full trial, not a plea deal. "It's not so much that I'm taking an opinion on life or death for these prisoners, but I believe in the judicial system and I believe that the process works and I believe that a trial and discovery and sort of a public airing is the way to flush the truth out," he said. Eagleson described the situation on Guantanamo as "a mess" and said he had decided not to attend any of the pre-trial proceedings there. "My overall feeling is a sense of betrayal from the US government and a sense of extreme frustration," he said. "They've botched every single part of this trial." With 25 years having passed since the attacks, he said that while 9/11 was a constant presence in his own life, to the wider public it was "becoming a historical event". "I think people just assume that we got Bin Laden, we're out of Iraq, the war in Afghanistan's over, and they just assume that chapter has ended." When the trial does eventually start, at a military court at Guantanamo, it has been estimated that it will last about a year. Professor Kasey McCall-Smith said the point of the pre-trial proceedings had been determining "what evidence gets in and what evidence doesn't get in". "If that is agreed in advance, the trial can be more expeditious," she explained. As the relatives of the victims prepared for another anniversary marking the death of their loved ones, Gerhardt said he was looking forward to a time that the trial was over and he no longer had to think about or travel to Guantanamo. "It's a place I don't want to come back to. I want to live my life, enjoy my passions and my memories of Ralph," he said.

item.title: Renoir paintings worth millions stolen in French museum heist
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c70drp0pyw2o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Renoir paintings worth millions stolen in French museum heist - Published Two paintings by the impressionist artist Pierre-Auguste Renoir have been stolen from a museum in the south of France. Two thieves broke into the Renoir Museum in Cagnes-sur-Mer early on Tuesday, seizing four paintings but dropping two of the works in the museum gardens as they escaped, local Mayor Bryan Masson said. The paintings, each worth €9m (£7.7m; $10.4m), are the latest high-profile pieces to have been stolen in a string of recent heists in Europe which have thrust the security of art in galleries and museums into the spotlight. One of the most high-profile was in October last year, when a brazen heist at the Louvre Museum in Paris saw France's priceless crown jewels being stolen. CCTV footage captured the thieves entering the Renoir museum gardens by cutting through a fence before they cut through structures holding the paintings' frames in place, the local mayor said. The alarm went off at 05:48 (03:48 GMT), and police were at the scene within five minutes, Masson explained, saying the thieves fled the scene upon hearing the security alarms. He later told reporters that the thieves seemed to be "well-equipped" and "well-informed". They were "wearing helmets, gloves, and combat gear" and carrying "an electric knife and hacksaw," he added. Investigators have found two zip-up bags at the scene, which may have belonged to the suspects. The mayor said that two paintings were "abandoned" in the gardens and have now been recovered. The two paintings that are still missing are: - Portrait of Madame Colonna Romano (1910) - Jeune fille au puits (1886) And the two pieces that were recovered are: - Portrait of Madame Pichon (1895) - Coco Lisant (1905) "Attacking the Renoir Museum is attacking a part of the history and heritage of Cagnes-sur-Mer," the mayor told reporters at the museum. "It's Renoir's, it is priceless, you cannot sell it like that," he said. The Renoir Museum is home to 12 of the famous painter's artworks. Opened in 1960, it was Renoir's last home before his death in 1919, and also features many things that once belonged to him, including his easel and wheelchair, as well as photographs and personal letters. Last month, four Renaissance paintings were stolen from a museum in Sicily. "Beyond Cagnes-sur-Mer, this incident should serve as a warning about the protection of our museums, which now face a new form of organised crime targeting works of art," the local French mayor warned. Masson called on the French government to provide more financial support to local areas and museums to protect artwork from "increasingly organised and determined criminals". - Published16 August - Published20 October 2025

item.title: Meta continues to run ads promoting child sexual abuse material in India - report
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqxv2vwjjq3o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Meta continues to run ads promoting child sexual abuse material in India - report - Published Warning: This story contains descriptions of abuse Meta ran hundreds of paid ads with artificial intelligence-generated child sexual abuse imagery, including several in India, over the past 10 months, a new report by US-based campaigners has found. The report comes two months after the Indian government ordered Meta to remove all ads and content promoting child sexual abuse material (CSAM) on Instagram. This was in the aftermath of a BBC Eye investigation which found that Instagram was running paid adverts promoting CSAM in India. Washington-based Tech Transparency Project (TTP), external says it found 332 adverts with CSAM that ran on Facebook and Instagram, the majority of them (274) in August this year. When the BBC wrote to Meta about these findings, they said in a statement, "We don't tolerate nudify apps or any kind of child exploitation, whether real or AI-generated. These criminals constantly shift tactics to evade detection, which is why we keep strengthening our detection and enforcement." The TTP report, published on Tuesday, says that it identified several photos of real children, including a member of a European royal family, that were used in the ads and then manipulated using AI. It says more than a dozen ads appeared on Meta platforms even after TTP made the company aware of its findings. About a quarter (84) of the ads ran in India and 78 of these were published after the Indian government's order on removing CSAM and its meeting with senior Meta officials. After the BBC investigation, several Indian agencies including the National Commission for Protection of Child Rights and the National Human Rights Commission have said they are examining the matter. The distribution of CSAM is a criminal offence in India, while Meta's policy states that ads must not contain content that sexually exploits or endangers children. When the BBC contacted Meta about its investigation, it said that when it becomes aware of apparent child exploitation, it reports it to the US-based National Center for Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC) in compliance with its legal obligations. The NCMEC is the centralised global reporting system for the online sexual exploitation of children. But Bhuwan Ribhu, the founder of Just Rights for Children, a network of more than 250 organisations working to prevent violence against children in India, says this is not enough. Just Rights for Children has filed a petition in India's Supreme Court, citing the BBC's findings, and asked for directions to social media platforms for mandatory reporting and identification of those promoting child sexual abuse material "Social media companies are clearly flouting Indian laws by not reporting child sexual abuse content to Indian law enforcement agencies as mandated by our child protection laws," said Ribhu. The TTP, a research initiative of the non-profit Campaign for Accountability that seeks to hold large technology companies accountable, said it found 332 ads featuring CSAM on Instagram and Facebook running in the US, UK, EU, Australia and India. They say they have reported all the ads to NCMEC. According to TTP, almost all the ads they found start with a photo of a child, and, as the video plays, the photo is manipulated by AI to show them engaging in a graphic sexual act. TTP described one ad which ran in India as: A photo of a preteen girl animated so that she performs a graphic sex act, with a voiceover that says, "There are no restrictions. All the characters are real people and there are many options. This is the AI men actually use." The BBC has not seen this ad. According to TTP, the ad was posted by more than 50 different handles in India over a fortnight in August this year. In July, after BBC's investigation, Meta had put out a detailed post on its website, external about how it fights child exploitation on its apps. "Anyone on our platforms can report ads if they believe they violate our policies," it said. TTP said that it tried reporting ads via Meta's own reporting system and that of the 84 ads that ran in India, they were able to report 55. Meta only gives the option of reporting ads when they are live. For 43 of these, TTP got a reply that said, "We've taken a look and found that this ad doesn't go against our Advertising Standards." For 11 ads, they were told that the content had already been removed. They haven't received a response yet for one ad. When the BBC reached out to Meta for a comment, they said, "we've built strong defenses, including systems that block violating ads as well as ongoing monitoring in case we initially miss something: that's why many of the ads flagged to us had already been removed, most had fewer than 200 impressions, and the total ad spend was under $5,000". TTP said that when it reached out to Meta for a response, all the ads they reported were removed. This was similar to what happened during the BBC's investigation. When the BBC used Meta's reporting system to report one of the ads featuring child sexual abuse to Instagram, the platform did not take it down. Later, when the BBC asked Meta for comment, it said it had already disabled several adverts and suspended the accounts posting them. The company said it had removed additional ads, disabled more accounts and blocked URLs for other content that violated its policies in response to the BBC's findings. TTP said that the vast majority of the 332 ads they found directed users to AI image or video generation apps, mostly from Chinese developers. The report alleged that by advertising these apps using images of child sexual abuse, the implication is that they can be used for creating or viewing CSAM. Meta has said it prohibits, external promotion of nudify apps, which use AI to create fake non-consensual nude or sexually explicit images. One of India's top cyber police officers, Shikha Goel, who is director of the Cyber Security Bureau in the Indian state of Telangana, told the BBC that one of the biggest challenges with CSAM is "the ease with which users can move from one platform to another, making it harder to nab them". "We are hopeful that the government will be addressing this in its latest interactions with social media intermediaries and direct them accordingly," she added. The ads that BBC had found in its investigation also directed users to another app - the messaging app Telegram - where they could buy the material for as little as 99 rupees [$1.05; £0.80]. Telegram told the BBC at the time that the company uses both automated and human moderation to tackle CSAM, and that it has "virtually eliminated the public spread of CSAM" on its platform. Ads on Meta's platforms are only published after first being approved by its moderation technology. Its review system relies primarily on automation and is designed to check images, video, text and audio, as well as who the ad is targeting and where links send them to. After the BBC's investigation, Meta had said that "no system is perfect" and that "determined criminals continue to try to exploit our platform, including through our advertising systems". But TTP found that several of the ads featuring child sexual abuse were placed by Meta's own ad agency partners in China. These partners, known as "resellers", channel billions of dollars' worth of Chinese advertising onto Facebook and Instagram. The partners did not respond to TTP's questions. TTP said that new ads have continued to appear even after they made Meta aware of their report's findings. They shared details of 17 ads including 11 that ran in India on 1-2 September.

item.title: Ukrainian TV channel building hit by Russian drone as five killed in Kyiv
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cn8m1k7p3v7o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Ukrainian TV channel building hit by Russian drone as five killed in Kyiv - Published A Russian drone has struck a Ukrainian TV channel headquarters in Kyiv, injuring at least five people as journalists were broadcasting live, President Volodymyr Zelensky has said. Zelensky said the daytime attack was a "new page in Russian degradation", while photos shared by the president showed a partially collapsed building. At least five people have been killed in overnight and daytime Russian strikes on Kyiv. A separate attack on a passenger train in southern Ukraine killed a female employee, officials have said. Both countries had earlier agreed to halt strikes on each other's capitals for three days while US Donald Trump's top envoys visited Moscow and Kyiv over the weekend. Referring to Tuesday's Russian drone attack on the Ukrainian TV channel We Are Ukraine, Zelensky said: "Today, Russia carried out a strike on the media, journalists. "Russia must be stopped, and this is possible only through joint efforts," he added in a renewed plea to Ukraine's allies in Europe, the US and around the world. We Are Ukraine has published footage which it says shows the moment the drone hit its newsroom. "The footage confirms that this was not an accidental strike, but a deliberate attack targeting journalists," the channel said in a post on Telegram. A BBC team later visited the site, confirming that the TV channel's newsroom was damaged in the strike, which reportedly interrupted the live broadcast. Earlier on Tuesday, air raid alerts warned civilians to seek shelter as Russian forces carried out missile and drone strikes on Kyiv, the local authorities said. A series of explosions across Ukraine's capital overnight killed three people and injured another 25, the state emergencies service DSNS said. Residential buildings were hit, including a five-storey house in the Solomianskyi district, while vehicles caught fire in the Podilskyi district. People sought shelter inside a metro station in Kyiv during the overnight attack, something that is routine for residents protecting themselves during the ongoing war. By Tuesday afternoon, the death toll had reached five people. According to a BBC Verify analysis, Kyiv is suffering more daily air raid alerts than at any time since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022. In Russia, buildings were struck in the city of Saratov during a Ukrainian drone attack, its regional governor Roman Busargin said early on Tuesday. The talks with Trump's top envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner in Moscow and Kyiv ended without any major breakthroughs. On Tuesday evening, Russian President Vladimir Putin and his US counterpart Donald Trump held a "constructive and very frank" talks on the phone, Moscow said. The two leaders spoke for an hour, Putin's senior adviser Yuriy Ushakov said. The Trump administration has not publicly commented, while Witkoff earlier had said that "substantive progress was made", without giving any further details. Ushakov had said on Saturday that Trump's envoys were informed in Moscow about "the significant advances made by the Russian armed forces" on the battlefield and stressed that the Kremlin's "set objectives would be achieved". Meanwhile, Zelensky said he expected the war to continue into the winter after meeting Witkoff and Kushner in Kyiv on Sunday - their first ever visit to Ukraine. Zelensky told reporters they had agreed that officials from Ukraine, Europe and America would meet in the near future to continue discussions. He also called for a trilateral meeting with Russia and the US. Putin has so far showed no sign of backing down from his maximalist demands, which included more territorial concessions from Ukraine.

item.title: Argentina to file criminal case against oil company operating in Falklands
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c8jd14glvneo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Argentina to file criminal case against oil company operating in Falklands - Published The Argentine government has said that it will file criminal charges against oil company Navitas Petroleum for operating in seas off the Falkland Islands. The move came just days after Argentine President Javier Milei said he would sanction oil companies drilling in the British overseas territory in the south-west Atlantic Ocean. Reacting to the news, Foreign Office Minister Kirsty McNeill insisted that there could be "no doubt" about the British government's commitment to the Falkland Islanders. Sovereignty of the archipelago remains disputed between the UK and Argentina more than 40 years after a British military task force ejected Argentine forces which had invaded the territory in 1982. Speaking in the House of Commons on Tuesday, McNeill said that "the decision by the Falkland Islands government to pursue hydrocarbon production is a commercial decision for them to take alongside the commercial companies involved". She added that "the future of the Falkland Islands is for Falkland Islanders to determine". The simmering dispute between Britain and Argentina over the Falklands heated up last week, when Milei said in a speech to the nation that the "winds of change" favoured Argentina's claim to the islands. Milei has, in the past, been criticised by Argentine veterans of the 1982 conflict for being "too soft" on the Falklands, which Argentines call Las Malvinas. In his speech on Thursday evening local time, Milei restated his government's position on the territory, saying "the Malvinas are Argentine, historically and legally... there's no debate about that." The president described drilling for oil in the archipelago as a "clear and urgent danger" to Argentine sovereignty. He also dismissed the result of a 2013 referendum in which 99.8% of the islands' residents voted in favour of the Falklands remaining a British oversees territory. Milei argued that they were living on land which had been "usurped" by the British and therefore "have no legitimate right to self-determination". The British government dismissed Milei's speech and stressed that its position on the Falklands was "unwavering". Hopes that Milei's primetime speech may have been a blip and that he would return to his previous stance of strengthening diplomatic ties with the UK were crushed on Monday, however, when his office announced it would file criminal charges against Navitas Petroleum, several of its subsidiaries and their executives. Navitas, which is listed in Tel Aviv, holds a 65% stake in Sea Lion, an offshore oil project set to start production in the North Falkland Basin in 2028. The Sea Lion oilfield, around 130 miles (209 km) from the Falkland Islands, contains an estimated 1.7 billion barrels of oil. In Monday's statement, Milei alleged that drilling in the area would violate Argentine law banning resource exploitation without approval from the Argentine authorities. "The state will continue to pursue actions deemed necessary to counter any act which breaches the sovereign rights of the Argentine Republic," the statement insisted. Navitas has not yet responded to this latest statement but said last week that Milei's remarks were "not expected to have a material effect on the development activities of the Sea Lion Project, including the timetable for completion of the Project's development". Rockhopper, which owns a partial stake in the Sea Lion project, has also not yet commented on Milei's statement. Both companies have in the past stressed that Sea Lion holds valid licences from the Falkland Islands. Related topics - Published3 days ago

item.title: British widow faces deportation from Sweden after 22 years
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c62k0d4px6ro?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
British widow faces deportation from Sweden after 22 years - Published A 78-year-old British widow has told the BBC she is struggling to eat or sleep as the Swedish government threatens to deport her over a late post-Brexit residence application. Joyce Thomas, a retired nurse, moved to Sweden 22 years ago with her husband, who passed away from cancer three years ago. The threat of deportation came after Swedish authorities said they should have made a formal application to stay in the country after Brexit. Thomas has since had numerous applications and appeals rejected, and Tuesday marks the latest deadline for her to leave voluntarily. "This is absolute hell," she said from her home in Sweden. "I can't sleep, I can't eat. You get up in the morning, you don't know what's going to happen." The Swedish migration minister told the BBC that the government would "examine whether there are measures we can take to make the process easier for those affected" by some consequences of the EU-UK withdrawal agreement. When the UK left the EU on 31 January 2020, British citizens stopped being EU citizens, which meant they could no longer stay in Sweden with right of residence status. During a transitional period, British citizens could apply for residence status under the withdrawal agreement between the UK and the EU - which ended on 31 December 2021. Thomas said she and her husband were unaware that they needed to submit an application and she was only informed of the rule once she attempted to re-enter the country in 2023. After years of appeals, the Migrationsverket, the Swedish government agency responsible for migration, told her last month that her voluntary departure deadline was 8 September. Her lawyers are arguing against the deportation, but she is still waiting to hear from the government. Thomas said the possibility of having to leave her son, grandchildren, friends and husband's grave has become too much to bear. "I'm tired, I really am tired and I'm not young anymore," she said. "Where is the empathy? I've lived here for more than 20 years - I've got friends, I've got family." According to Eurostat data, between 2021 and 2025, 2,490 UK nationals were ordered to leave Sweden. This is almost a third of more than 7,500 UK nationals ordered to leave the 27 EU Member States over this time period. The Migrationsverket said it could not comment on Thomas's case without her consent and did not respond to a question about how many British nationals are at risk of deportation. However, it told the Guardian last week that 458 British citizens had been deported or forcibly removed since Brexit. Last month, a family told the BBC how their father, who has dementia and vascular parkinsonism and is living in full-time care in Sweden, was also threatened with removal after more than two decades in the country. Swedish Minister for Migration, Johan Forssell, told the BBC that the current framework was implemented by a previous government and that it "will therefore look closely at the situation and examine whether there are measures we can take to make the process easier for those affected". He did not address Thomas's case directly but said "the government believes the rules should be applied generously". "The UK is a very important partner for Sweden, and we want British citizens who live and work in Sweden to be able to remain here," he said. "We are currently in dialogue with the relevant Swedish authorities to get a clearer picture of what measures may be possible," he added. Håkan Svenneling, Thomas's MP from the opposition Vänsterpartiet (The Left Party), has criticised the government's "inhumane migration policy". "That is why I hope that Sunday's election in Sweden will be a turning point where the opposition can form a government and change migration policy so that Joyce and other Britons with strong ties to Sweden can stay here," he told the BBC. A spokesperson from the the UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office said: "We welcome the statement from the Swedish authorities that they will look at this issue. We are ready to support them in doing so." - Published22 August

item.title: Saudi Arabia vows to respond after Houthis attack cities and energy facilities
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cp849n2nz01o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Saudi Arabia vows to respond after Houthis attack cities and energy facilities - Published Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi movement has attacked energy facilities and other civilian infrastructure in Saudi Arabia with dozens of drones and missiles, injuring 73 people, Saudi authorities say. Tuesday's attacks hit four south-western cities, causing fires at oil facilities and installations that led to a temporary halt in operations, according to Saudi Arabia's military and energy ministry. The Saudi-led coalition in Yemen said that its forces would respond to the "dangerous escalation". The Houthis said the attacks were retaliation for dozens of recent Saudi strikes on areas of north-western Yemen that they control. On Monday, they accused Saudi Arabia of bombing a prison in the city of al-Hazm and killing at least 11 people. Twenty inmates are reportedly missing under the rubble. The spokesman for the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen, Maj Gen Turki al-Maliki, said the Houthi drone and missile attacks targeted civilian and economic sites in the cities of Abha, Khamis Mushait, Jazan and Najran, and that women and children were among the injured. An energy ministry statement cited an official source as saying that injuries were also reported after "several energy sector facilities and installations" were targeted. The attacks "caused fires at several locations, leading to a temporary halt in some operations," they added. Maliki described Houthi attacks as a "dangerous escalation that confirms the hostile and irresponsible approach of this terrorist militia" and said the Saudi-led coalition would "take all necessary operational measures to deter" the group. Houthi military spokesman Yahya Sarea accused the Saudi military of carrying out more than 120 air strikes on the Yemeni provinces of Marib, al-Bayda, Hudaydah, Taiz and Jawf over the past three days, and of committing "grave crimes". He said the Houthis had responded to this "brutal aggression" with "dozens of ballistic missiles and drones", which he claimed caused "significant damage". A Saudi-led coalition of Arab states has backed Yemen's government against the Houthis in the country's devastating civil war for more than a decade. A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea. The Houthis said they were retaliating for a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom. There has been heavy fighting on Yemen's south-western coast since Thursday, when the Houthis launched an offensive against Yemeni pro-government forces in a bid to take control of the Bab al-Mandab Strait, which connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden. The fighting has reportedly left more than 300 people dead and displaced 18,500. The Red Sea has become crucial for oil shipments from Saudi Arabia during the US and Israel's war with Iran, which has led to the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz in the Gulf.

item.title: Fourteen go on trial over deadliest Channel small boats disaster
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cd94jn72w2yo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Fourteen go on trial over deadliest Channel small boats disaster - Published Fourteen suspected people smugglers have gone on trial in Paris for their role in the worst ever small boats disaster in the English Channel. In November 2021, at least 30 men, women and children drowned when their motorised dinghy deflated and started taking on water halfway between France and the UK. The 14 defendants – mainly Afghan nationals – are accused of manslaughter and facilitating illegal immigration as part of an organised criminal group. Most of them deny the charges. Two of the 14, who are alleged to be leaders of the operation, remain on the run and are being tried in absentia. The boat left the French coast on the evening of 23 November 2021, but ran into difficulty in the middle of the Channel. One by one the occupants entered the water to try to lessen the weight, but succumbed to the cold and drowned. Only two men survived. According to the charge sheet, the defendants helped to launch "a small boat of poor quality, unfit to navigate at sea, overloaded and equipped with inadequate life-jackets". Twenty-seven bodies were found after the boat sank, and another four were confirmed missing. Many of the people who died were Iraqi Kurds, but others came from Somalia, Ethiopia, Egypt and Afghanistan. The youngest named victim was seven years old. Some family members travelled to Paris for the start of the trial, which is expected to last three weeks. "Once again [the smugglers displayed] total cynicism. Migrants are not sailors," said Emmanuel Daoud, a lawyer representing many of the families. "The smugglers know perfectly well what they are doing. They take the deliberate, conscious risk of sending migrants to their deaths." The defendants are accused of helping to organise the ill-fated journey by lodging and transporting the migrants, supplying the boat they left in, and handling the money they paid. But many of them insist that they were themselves migrants and that if they were involved it was only under instructions from the real organisers. The disaster led to enquiries on both sides of the Channel, with questions asked about the failure of British and French boats to rescue the people who died despite repeated calls from the floundering dinghy. In France, seven military personnel – staff at a maritime rescue centre and on board a navy boat - are under judicial investigation on a possible charge of failing to assist persons in danger. A judge will decide whether they should stand trial. A UK inquiry found that HM Coastguard in Dover had limited capacity due to chronic staff shortages, while a surveillance aircraft was not launched due to poor weather conditions. It also found that there was a widely held belief that migrants calling from small boats exaggerated the distress, meaning the coastguard underestimated the emergency. item.title: New Yorkers were 'lied' to about toxic air after 9/11 attacks, says Mamdani
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cjdvyk3pm27o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
New Yorkers were 'lied' to about toxic air after 9/11 attacks, says Mamdani - Published Toxic air quality was being recorded in Manhattan soon after the 9/11 attacks even as officials played down health risks to the public, according to a trove of newly released files. Asbestos was found "nearly everywhere" tested near Ground Zero, where the World Trade Center towers collapsed in 2001, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said. "People got sick because the leaders they trusted lied and told them they were safe to breathe in toxic air," he said, announcing the release of 170,000 documents related to the attacks. Illnesses related to the dust and smoke from the towers' collapse have claimed more lives than the nearly 3,000 who died in the attacks, US health officials say. Thousands of people have experienced health effects like cancer, including many who have died, after breathing in hazardous contaminants after the Twin Towers collapsed. Speaking alongside Mamdani at Tuesday's news conference, TV host and 9/11 survivor advocate Jon Stewart said the new files show the city knew by October 2001 - a month after the terrorist attacks - that the air in Manhattan was toxic. "So to be fair to them, they only buried that information for 25 years," he said sarcastically. The records show asbestos was found near Ground Zero for months after the attacks at the same time people were being advised it was safe to go there. The files, which include air-quality reports and communications among city officials, include October 2001 correspondence known as the "Harding Memo". In it, an aide warned former Deputy Mayor Robert Harding that the city could face as many as 35,000 legal claims for its response to the attacks. The document states that the city could be sued because health advisories caused individuals "to return to the area too soon (causing toxic exposure or emotional harm)". City officials also told citizens to clean up dust and debris with "wet mops and rags" despite the presence of asbestos, which is only supposed to be cleaned by licensed professionals, according to another memo documenting the concerns of congressman Jerry Nadler. The memo pointed to testimony from the city's top health official at the time saying a study had found "no elevated levels of asbestos in indoor air", but that tests showed dust had "low levels of asbestos in some samples". The memo, attributed to Ester Fuchs, a special adviser at the time to Mayor Michael Bloomberg, acknowledged "potential problems for City Hall". Days after the attack, city and federal officials - including the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) - declared that the air near the Twin Towers was safe. Christine Todd Whitman, the head of the EPA at the time, later apologised for this declaration, saying the agency "did the very best we could at the time with the knowledge we had". - Firefighter describes emotional 9/11 stair climb - Published2 days ago - Toxic dust legacy of 9/11 plagues thousands of people - Published1 September 2011 Tuesday's release of documents resolves a lawsuit brought by advocacy group 9/11 Health Watch, which sued after officials said they did not have the records. City officials found 68 boxes of documents last year. The pages of air quality reports and other records were released through an online portal timed for this Friday's 25th anniversary of the attacks. More documents are to be shared over the next year. Karen Klingon, who was involved in the 9/11 Health Watch lawsuit, told the BBC on Tuesday her brother lived five minutes away from Ground Zero. He developed asthma, was later diagnosed with cancer and died at 61 of a related brain tumor. "There's a lot of research, probably, that can be done about what was in the air, and the kind of illnesses that derived of those toxins that were in the air, like what happened to my brother," she said. "Hopefully it helps people that were sick know and in the future." Phil Alvarez, whose brother Luis Alvarez died of cancer in 2019 after exposure to Ground Zero toxins, told the BBC that people "continue to get sick every single day, continue to die".

item.title: LIV files for bankruptcy protection with over $45m owed to players
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/golf/articles/ce8x39wj5p1o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
LIV files for bankruptcy protection with over $45m owed to players - Published LIV Golf has filed for bankruptcy protection with at least $45m (£33m) owed to players, who will now have the option to leave. A Chapter 11 petition, which LIV says is to "preserve the company's business" as it attempts to restructure after Saudi Arabia withdrew its multibillion-dollar funding, was filed in the United States on Tuesday. The breakaway league says it has found a new investor in BC Partners, following the decision in April by Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund (PIF) to pull its funding. Documents in the petition outline money owed to LIV Golf's creditors with the 30 largest unsecured claims. Two-time major winner Jon Rahm tops that list with an unsecured claim of $7.5m (£5.5m). Bryson DeChambeau ($5.7m - £4.2m), Dustin Johnson ($5.5m - £4.1m), Cameron Smith ($4.8m - £3.5m) and Tyrrell Hatton ($3.4m - £2.5m) are also among the top 30 creditors, as well as Brooks Koepka, who left to rejoin the PGA Tour in January but has an unsecured claim of $1.7m (£1.25m). The total amount owed to the 14 current and former LIV players in the top 30 creditors is just over $45m (£33m). A source familiar with the figures told BBC Sport the creditors list outlines the "amount owed and not paid for Q3" of 2026, not the full amounts. The court documents show LIV estimates its assets at $100m-$500m (£74m-£370m) and its liabilities at between $500m and $1bn (£370m-£739m). LIV Golf intends to commence its new majority player-owned league early next year and it is understood the Chapter 11 process allows it to start talking to players about their participation in LIV's future. BBC Sport understands there is no obligation on players to sign on to LIV 2.0, regardless of whether they had previously signed multi-year contracts with LIV Golf. Sources have said contracts under the previous iteration of LIV Golf will finish because of this court filing, with amounts owed to players and other creditors addressed through the court process. However, it remains unclear when players would then be able to enter discussions with other tours. - 'Time will tell' - Rahm on LIV Golf future - Published15 hours ago - Strained smiles and uncertainty - the strange end of LIV Golf 1.0 - Published21 August - Saudi Arabia to stop funding LIV Golf next season - Published30 April Since LIV's controversial launch in 2021, more than $5bn (£3.7bn) has been spent by PIF, with major winners including Rahm and DeChambeau lured by lucrative contracts and vast prize money. However, the future of the concept - and its star players - has been shrouded in uncertainty, with the 2026 season having ended early. LIV Golf chief executive Scott O'Neil told the BBC at the final event in Indianapolis last month he had "high levels of confidence" in achieving a "critical mass" of players to make the new league a reality. DeChambeau said at the conclusion of that event he felt there was "a lot of potential moving forward" and he believed there was "something fun coming". Speaking on Tuesday before this week's Irish Open, Rahm was tight-lipped when pressed on his future. Asked if he knew what the coming months held, he told BBC Sport: "Yes and no. It hasn't really changed from my last interview in Indianapolis. "There's just a lot of things in place, right? There's a lot of things that could happen and it's one of those things where time's gonna tell." Rahm added: "I still have a contract with LIV 1.0 that I'm more than willing to fulfil, so like I said, time will tell." The bankruptcy filing was made in the federal district court of New Jersey, where LIV Golf set up a subsidiary earlier in the summer. Chapter 11 protection postpones a US company's obligations to its creditors, giving it time to reorganise its debts or sell parts of the business. PIF is providing a bankruptcy loan of $49.6m (£36.6m) - called 'debtor in possession' (DIP) financing - to help fund the process. When announcing its decision to withdraw funding, PIF said the "substantial investment required by LIV Golf over a longer term" was "no longer consistent" with its strategy. Despite its decision to stop bankrolling LIV Golf, PIF added it "remains committed" to its "substantial current and future investments in various sports as a priority sector". On Tuesday, LIV confirmed international investment firm BC Partners as its proposed new investor in a letter to fans outlining its "next phase". "LIV Golf has entered a court-supervised restructuring process that provides us with the time and framework to address previous financial obligations and complete a transaction that will make the league's next phase a reality," said the letter. "Put simply, this process is designed to build a stronger and more sustainable future for LIV Golf." O'Neil added in a statement: "This process gives us the structure and time to pursue a landmark transaction and begin the next chapter of LIV Golf - one built around the fans, an innovative, player-first ownership model, and a part of the global golf ecosystem." In yet another indication the free-spending days of LIV 1.0 are over, the letter said the new league would be "built around a sustainable business model". Players are set to be given equity and individual commercial rights are set to be returned to players, giving them greater earning potential. In terms of prize money, LIV Golf purses are set to be lower than events on the PGA Tour - which has risen in part because of the existence of LIV - but higher than events on the DP World Tour. The letter also outlined proposed changes, with field sizes expanding to 75 players, the introduction of a cut, creating qualifiers and having more teams that "embrace national identities", with the ambitions for teams to "grow into enduring global sports businesses". item.title: Sudan's healthcare system on brink of collapse after cuts, medical charity warns
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c62m8247yleo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Sudan's healthcare system on brink of collapse after cuts, medical charity warns - Published Sudan's fragile health system is on the brink of collapse as global funding cuts have led to the closure of healthcare facilities across the country, Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) has warned. Dozens of organisations were unable to find alternative funding after the US - the largest donor to Sudan - closed USAID, its body for delivering foreign aid, last year, the medical charity said. MSF urged world leaders gathering at the UN General Assembly in New York to take action. The war that erupted in April 2023 between the army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) has created one of the worst humanitarian crises in the world, with more than 33 million people needing medical assistance. MSF said while the US was still the largest donor to Sudan, existing grants to many USAID-funded organisations ran out in June - as European governments were also reducing international assistance. According to the Paris-based Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), international aid fell globally by 21.3% in 2025 compared to the previous year. - A simple guide to what is happening in Sudan - Published13 November 2025 - Sudan's invisible children - born in war with no legal identity - Published7 August "War is driving Sudan's needs; funding cuts are shrinking the response," said Muhammad Ibrahim, the head of charity in Sudan. "MSF's work in Sudan is privately funded. But when funding disappears from other health services, clinics close, patients have fewer places to go, and pressure shifts to the facilities that remain, including ours." This has meant that patients often have to make dangerous and long trips to get treatment. "After a longer and more expensive journey, patients often arrive in a much more serious condition, and the hospital may already be full," explained Sebastián Traficante, MSF's emergency co-ordinator in the western region of Darfur, which has experienced much of the fighting over the last three years. Between January and April 2026, MSF saw admissions jump by 22.5% in facilities it supports in central Darfur, when compared to the same time last year. In May alone, 45 healthcare centres in the area had stopped receiving funding, it said. According to MSF, the closure of frontline services was putting other hospitals under severe strain - as they were losing their capacity to function and medicines were disappearing. It gave Gedaref state's Tanedba camp, where 18,400 people who have fled their homes live, as an example. Its maternity and surgical wards have closed down after a humanitarian organisation left in June. As a result, MSF is now running an emergency room there, but pregnant women who need surgery to deliver a baby, have to travel three hours to the nearest city. In the Um Rakuba camp - also in Gedaref - the number of aid agencies working there has dropped from 35 in 2021, to less than 10. According to the charity, the camp currently hosts around 17,000 people, most of whom are women and children. "If support does not increase, more patients will face longer journeys, fewer treatment options and greater risk of arriving too late for care," MSF's UK humanitarian representative Liz Harding said. At the same time as the health system was struggling with funding, attacks on healthcare workers were continuing, MSF said. In 2025, Sudan saw 1,620 people killed in attacks on medical facilities - which the charity said accounted for 82% of all global deaths from attacks on healthcare worldwide. According to the UN, more than 19.5 million people are also experiencing "crisis levels" of food insecurity and more than five million are facing "emergency levels of hunger". The fighting shows no sign of easing - despite the expected arrival of international diplomats in the Sudanese capital, Khartoum, for consultations aimed at ending the civil war. Reports from North Kordofan state on Tuesday say at least 11 people have been killed in a drone attack on the army-controlled town of Umm Ruwaba. According to medical sources, the projectile struck a crowded courtyard in a court complex.
